prompt: Which of the five kinds of lock-in is the only one with an end date written on it?
hint: One of them is signed for one or three years.

choices.text: The API surface
choices.why: Code shaped by bindings or a workflow definition keeps that shape until somebody rewrites it.

choices.text: The data
choices.why: Data gets heavier every month it stays, and no date ends that.

choices.text: A contract
choices.why: Right: a reservation or a savings plan of one or three years. It is also the only kind that is purely financial.

choices.text: Operations
choices.why: What a team knows fades slowly and on no calendar, and its tools stay until replaced.

prompt: Match each kind of lock-in to the shop's example of it.
hint: Code, data, Entra, people, signature.

pairs.right: A function decorated with a queue trigger
Role assignments naming a managed identity
Saved queries and three people's reflexes

right_distractors: A bug in the shop's order handler

prompt: The shop no longer needs a reservation it bought, nor a savings plan. What does Microsoft's documentation say it can do?
hint: The two commitments are not equally firm.

choices.text: Cancel both and get a pro-rated refund of each
choices.why: Only the reservation can be returned. A savings plan purchase is final.

choices.text: Exchange the savings plan for a reservation it can use
choices.why: The documentation says a savings plan can't be exchanged for a reservation; the trade-in goes the other way.

choices.text: Neither: both are final once bought
choices.why: True of the savings plan, not of the reservation, which can be exchanged or refunded.

choices.text: Return the reservation, within a yearly cap, and keep paying for the plan
choices.why: Right: cancelled reservations may total up to 50,000 USD in a rolling twelve months, and a savings plan can't be cancelled.

prompt: Why does the lesson's figure leave data and identity out of its columns?
hint: Ask what they belong to.

choices.text: Neither of them causes any lock-in on Azure
choices.why: Both do, and the section gives each its own heading; they just do not vary by compute.

choices.text: They belong to what the code connects to, whatever runs it
choices.why: Right: the database weighs the same and the role assignments are the same whether Container Apps or AKS runs the code.

choices.text: A savings plan covers both, as it covers contracts
choices.why: A compute savings plan does not cover storage or identity at all.

choices.text: They only matter on virtual machines
choices.why: A Container App reading a database and using a managed identity carries both.

prompt: A pod on AKS gets Entra tokens through workload identity, as in lesson 13. If the cluster moves to another provider, which part travels with it?
hint: Who issued each of the two tokens?

choices.text: The federated credential, because it names the cluster
choices.why: It names the cluster's issuer, but it lives on a managed identity in Entra, and stays there.

choices.text: The projected service-account token
choices.why: Right: Kubernetes signs it, on any conformant cluster. The exchange for an access token is Entra's and stays behind.

choices.text: The access token for the storage account
choices.why: Entra issues it, for an Azure resource; it is the half that does not travel.

choices.text: The role assignment on the storage account
choices.why: Role assignments are Azure RBAC, held by Azure; another provider has its own model.

prompt: The shop ran on its own, beside Dapr and in kind. What showed that it was the same image each time?
hint: Not the tag: lesson 10 moved one.

choices.text: The same answer from /version, host name included
choices.why: The host name is the container's or the pod's, and it changed every time.

choices.text: The tag shop:1.0 in every command
choices.why: A tag is a name that can be moved to another image; it proves nothing about which bytes ran.

choices.text: The same sha256 digest
choices.why: Right: a hash of the image's own description, which changes if one byte of it changes.

choices.text: The same container id in all three runs
choices.why: Each run made a new container, with a new id; the image under them was the constant.

prompt: Which of these keep Azure out of the shop's code, or confine it to one place? Choose all that apply.
hint: A seam is something that moves with you, or one place the provider may appear.

choices.text: An OCI image built from a Dockerfile
choices.why: It ran three ways in this section; the file around it stays behind.

choices.text: Code instrumented with the OpenTelemetry API
choices.why: Azure appears only where the exporter is configured.

choices.text: Handlers that read the CloudEvents 1.0 envelope
choices.why: An open specification that Event Grid speaks, and other brokers do too.

choices.text: The Bicep files that declare the Container App
choices.why: Bicep declares Azure resources and nothing else; those files are rewritten on the way out.

choices.text: Functions decorated with a queue trigger
choices.why: Bindings are the Functions host's feature, and lesson 15 chose that lock-in on purpose.

prompt: Put in order what happens when curl asks the shop's sidecar for /version.
hint: From the laptop's port 3500 to the JSON that comes back.
items: daprd, in the shop's network, receives the request
daprd calls the app on localhost:8080/version
the shop answers, and daprd passes the JSON back
trap: Port 3500 was published on the shop's container, but it is daprd that listens on it, not app.py.

prompt: Terraform reaches many providers, but a Terraform file for the shop on Azure names ___ resources, which run nowhere else.
hint: The name of Terraform's Azure provider.

prompt: A team wraps Durable Functions in a workflow layer of its own, "so that we could move one day". What has it bought?
hint: Who maintains the layer on the days nobody moves?

choices.text: Nothing it did not have, since Durable Functions is portable
choices.why: Its orchestrators, their replay rules and their history in a storage account are Azure Functions'.

choices.text: A workflow engine to maintain every day it stays
choices.why: Right: the price of a seam grows with every feature you decide not to use directly.

choices.text: A Dapr sidecar in every replica of every app
choices.why: That is the price of lesson 9's abstraction, a different seam bought as a product.

choices.text: An image that will no longer run anywhere else
choices.why: A workflow layer is code; it does not change where the image runs.

prompt: At the example's illustrative 0.10 USD per GB, what does carrying 450 GB out of Azure cost, in USD?
hint: Gigabytes times the rate.

prompt: Why is the image's line zero person-days in the shop's estimate?
hint: Section 03 answered this before the estimate was made.

choices.text: It ran unchanged three ways, so nothing in it is Azure's
choices.why: Right: a seam already paid for. What moves is the file around it, which has its own line.

choices.text: Storing an image in a registry is free
choices.why: The line counts person-days to replace, not storage; and lesson 10's registry is not free.

choices.text: The program leaves rows of kind API out of the total
choices.why: It adds every row; the Container App and the queue are API too, and score 3 and 2.

choices.text: The image is rebuilt on the next platform anyway
choices.why: It does not need to be: the same digest ran under Docker, Dapr and Kubernetes.

prompt: The largest line of the shop's example estimate is not code: it is the ___ of three developers on another platform, twelve person-days.
hint: What people need before they can run the move.

prompt: Why does the estimate keep the full transfer rate, even if Microsoft might offer relief to a customer leaving?
hint: Which figure needs nobody to say yes?

choices.text: Relief is never offered to anybody
choices.why: The section does not say that; it says to ask on the day.

choices.text: It is the figure that holds without anybody's approval
choices.why: Right: an estimate built on a concession nobody has granted is a hope.

choices.text: The rate in the program is Azure's published one
choices.why: It is illustrative and labelled so; the real one comes from the calculator or the Retail Prices API.

choices.text: The data line is the largest in the estimate
choices.why: For the shop it is small; people are the largest line.

prompt: Which line of the estimate is counted from the old platform's monthly bill?
hint: Both platforms run while the move happens.

choices.text: Rewrite
choices.why: Rewrite is person-days per component touching Azure.

choices.text: Data
choices.why: Data is gigabytes times a rate per gigabyte.

choices.text: Retraining
choices.why: Retraining is people times days to learn.

choices.text: Overlap
choices.why: Right: months of running both, times what Azure costs a month meanwhile.

prompt: Put the parts of the shop's decision record in the order the file gives them.
hint: Who and when, why, what, then the prices and the ways out.
items: id, title, status, date and deciders
context: the traffic, the two jobs and the team
decision: Container Apps and two jobs
lock-in accepted, each with an exit
revisit when, and the review date
trap: Reading the triggers before the lock-in accepted means reading what would undo a choice before knowing the choice.

prompt: What is the exit: line beside each accepted lock-in for?
hint: It does not plan the whole move.

choices.text: A full migration plan, with dates and owners
choices.why: Too much to keep true in a record nobody edits; it names a first step and a size.

choices.text: The date on which that lock-in ends
choices.why: Only a contract has an end date; the review date is a separate field.

choices.text: The first step out and its size
choices.why: Right: so the answer to "what if we had to leave?" is already in the repository.

choices.text: Who must approve a pull request touching it
choices.why: The record names its deciders once, at the top; exits are about leaving, not reviewing.

prompt: A pull request imports the Service Bus client in the order handler. What does the record let a reviewer do?
hint: Read its lock-in refused lines.

choices.text: Reject it automatically, since the record runs in CI
choices.why: The record is a document and runs nowhere; a person reads it.

choices.text: Nothing, because a record describes only the past
choices.why: It describes the rules the team agreed to keep, which apply to every new change.

choices.text: Accept it, as Service Bus is accepted lock-in already
choices.why: The queue is accepted; the client outside its two modules is refused.

choices.text: Point at the refused line it crosses
choices.why: Right: and if the team wants the change, it needs a new record that says so.

prompt: When a new decision record takes the place of an older one, it ___ it, and the old record stays in the repository.
hint: Record 12 does this to record 7.

prompt: Which of these could stand as an exit trigger in a decision record? Choose all that apply.
hint: A trigger is something a dashboard can show.

choices.text: Traffic near three times today's for a month
choices.why: A request count an alert can watch.

choices.text: If Azure gets expensive
choices.why: Expensive compared with what, and by how much? Nobody can tell when it fired.

choices.text: Real rates leave Container Apps less than 20% cheaper
choices.why: A number lesson 21's program prints, with a threshold.

choices.text: When the team starts to feel locked in
choices.why: A mood, which is what section 02 set out to replace with a list.

choices.text: A second app that spends the free grants
choices.why: An event anybody can see in the subscription.

prompt: With the example's illustrative rates, the move takes three months instead of two, at 150 USD a month, and 600 GB leave instead of 300, at 0.10 USD per GB. What do the overlap and data lines add up to, in USD?
hint: Months times the bill, plus gigabytes times the rate.

prompt: Match each compute choice to what the lesson's table says about it.
hint: Read each row for its strongest kind.

pairs.right: Code shaped by bindings and the host
Kubernetes skills the team has to keep
A workflow and connectors one service runs
A Linux machine, the least Azure-shaped

right_distractors: A contract with no end date

prompt: Another team asks whether to put Dapr in front of Service Bus to stay portable. It has one app, one namespace and no plan to change broker. What do this lesson and lesson 9 suggest?
hint: A seam is worth paying for where leaving is likely or expensive.

choices.text: Adopt Dapr, which removes the lock-in entirely
choices.why: It moves the dependency to Dapr's API, and adds a sidecar and a hop to every replica.

choices.text: Use Logic Apps, which has no API lock-in
choices.why: Its workflow definition and connectors are among the most Azure-shaped things in the course.

choices.text: Run their own broker on virtual machines instead
choices.why: That is the opposite mistake: a monthly cost larger than most exits.

choices.text: The Service Bus library behind one function of their own
choices.why: Right: one place where the broker appears, and none of the sidecar's cost for a swap they will not make.

prompt: The shop's record says no savings plan before six months of steady traffic. Why wait?
hint: What happens to a savings plan the shop no longer needs?

choices.text: Savings plans do not cover Container Apps
choices.why: Microsoft's list includes Container Apps among the compute services a plan covers.

choices.text: A plan would add person-days to the exit estimate
choices.why: A contract adds money, not effort: nothing in the code changes.

choices.text: It can't be cancelled, so its size should come from measured traffic
choices.why: Right: six months show what the shop spends each hour, and the commitment is final once signed.

choices.text: Reservations are always cheaper than plans
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim; the two differ in what they commit to and how firm they are.
